extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers of mass communication, journalism, and media studies
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and influences that shape what news organizations choose to cover and how they present it, including economic, institutional, organizational, audience, advertiser, PR, and governmental forces. Useful for analyzing or producing news coverage and understanding media agenda-setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pseudoevent characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Boorstin's concept of a 'pseudoevent'—an occasion created primarily to be reported or reproduced by the media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Four defining features: (1) It is not spontaneous but planned, planted, or incited; (2) it is planted primarily for the immediate purpose of being reported or reproduced, arranged for the convenience of the media; (3) its relation to underlying reality is ambiguous—the interest often lies in that ambiguity rather than real consequences; (4) it is often intended to be a self-fulfilling prophecy (e.g., celebrating an anniversary to make an institution seem distinguished). Pseudoevents fulfill interest groups' need for coverage and the media's need for news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media demand for 'new' news
rubrics_metrics.description: Electronic news broadcasts and other media have an ongoing demand for 'new' news, driving continual production and coverage choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because audiences expect 'new' news at each broadcast and print deadlines produce continual demand, interest groups supply staged events to meet the media's need for fresh content—these staged items are more likely to be covered than some 'real' events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial content quantity determined by advertising (print)
rubrics_metrics.description: In print media, the amount of editorial content is largely determined by the amount of advertising content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The more ads a newspaper sells, the more editorial content it needs to 'put around the ads.' This economic linkage affects decisions about how much and what kind of editorial material is produced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial content constrained by time (electronic media)
rubrics_metrics.description: In electronic media, editorial content is limited by the fixed amount of broadcast time (minus advertising).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because available time is finite and audiences expect new items each broadcast, electronic outlets prioritize items that fit time constraints and the demand for novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public relations (PR) as a source and shaper of news
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations activities provide a wide range of materials (press releases to giant campaigns) and frequently serve as sources for news stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence on PR influence is mixed: some studies find substantial use of PIO-provided information and alignment of emphasis, others find limited uptake beyond organizations' news value. Journalists' and PR practitioners' news judgments are often similar. PR messages may have persuasive or cognitive goals (e.g., warning about hazards or educating the public).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trends in PR firms affecting media inputs
rubrics_metrics.description: Structural and procedural trends within the public relations industry that affect how PR interacts with media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three identified trends: (1) increasing consolidation of ownership among large firms (PR conglomerates like WPP, Omnicom); (2) growing internationalization (largest firms operate globally); (3) rising importance of market research as a decision-making tool, sometimes overshadowing personal contact and traditional communication tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermedia agenda-setting and imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations act as sources for one another; certain outlets set agendas that others follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some outlets (e.g., New England Journal of Medicine for medical news, The New York Times for general news, NPR programs, and wire services) often lead coverage. When one medium breaks a story, others pick it up; similarity in content across media may reflect shared news values as much as causal transmission from wire services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wire services' role and content homogeneity
rubrics_metrics.description: Wire services transmit stories that are widely republished, potentially acting as agenda setters and contributing to homogeneity across newspapers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies show newspapers often publish the same kinds of content in the same proportions as wire services transmit, although this may be due to shared notions of newsworthiness rather than direct causation; nonsubscribing newspapers sometimes give similar play to the same stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market/advertiser-driven target audience selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisers define and buy audiences, so media tailor content to attract the 'target audience' most valuable to advertisers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target audiences are defined by demographics (age, gender, income, education) and psychographics (attitudes, lifestyles). Media try to capture 'the right' audience by discovering what they want and providing it, sometimes shifting coverage to reach higher-value segments (e.g., 'upscale' readers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience as commodity (attention economics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Human attention is a commodity sold to advertisers; audience share translates directly into advertising revenue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because advertisers pay based on audience size and composition (e.g., cost per thousand), media organizations prioritize programming and content that will attract advertiser-valued audiences; a small change in audience share can represent large revenue changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailoring editions and content delivery technologies
rubrics_metrics.description: Technologies enable media to tailor editions or sections to subsets of subscribers so advertisers' messages reach likely buyers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailoring could allow subscribers to receive only sections they want, making advertising delivery more efficient; practical/mechanical challenges (labeling, distribution) exist, but planning for tailored delivery influences content packaging decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertisers' direct leverage and economic pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisers can and do use financial power to influence news coverage by threatening or withdrawing ad buys.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surveys show many editors have experienced advertiser threats or actual ad withdrawals in response to unfavorable coverage. As advertising revenue becomes crucial, there may be a move away from independent reporting toward greater reliance on press releases or advertiser-friendly content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate and sponsor influence beyond traditional ads
rubrics_metrics.description: Financial backers of programming—corporate sponsors, foundations—can shape content, even where traditional advertising is absent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: NPR's reliance on corporate and foundation sponsors has been argued to impair objectivity and make the network more ratings-conscious, fostering an 'establishment tone' and reliance on administrative sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertiser-created programming and product-driven content
rubrics_metrics.description: Programming conceived or produced by advertisers or manufacturers primarily to promote products (e.g., program-length commercials, advertiser-created shows).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such programming is often designed to provide product exposure, with manufacturers exercising creative control over characters, messages, and environments. This blurs editorial/advertising boundaries (e.g., children's shows built around toy lines, Macy's cable channel devoted to selling merchandise).

rubrics_metrics.name: Infomercials and long-form direct-response advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: The growth of infomercials and long-form television advertising that resembles programming and drives direct sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infomercials (30-minute formats) became prominent since the late 1980s, generating substantial ad revenue and often using celebrity endorsers and customer testimonials; they are programmed between regular programming and can be hard for viewers to distinguish from editorial content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blurring of advertising and editorial coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertising can cross into editorial space when news outlets cover ads or political spots as newsworthy items or when content is produced to gain news coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: networks leading evening news with political ads; campaigns producing material designed to be picked up as news. Editors may run favorable editorial coverage of major advertisers' products or people (e.g., Vanity Fair covering its advertisers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry-specific influence exemplars (e.g., tobacco)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain industries (historically tobacco) have exerted disproportionate influence over media content through advertising spending and other pressures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tobacco companies have a history of withdrawing ads, pressuring publishers, and underwriting product placement; editors may self-censor or reduce coverage of health risks to avoid angering advertisers or their corporate affiliates, even when editorial policy ostensibly opposes such influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience knowledge limits and newsroom socialization
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists' knowledge of and orientation toward their audience is uneven, affecting coverage choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circulation and advertising departments may provide a 'picture' of the audience, but reporters often lack deep understanding; minority journalists are not uniformly knowledgeable about their communities, and newsroom socialization draws attention toward advertiser-valued audiences, which can skew content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeted content for ethnic or niche audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Media may alter content to attract or retain ethnic and niche audiences in response to market opportunity and advertiser interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: mainstream outlets creating Latino-targeted inserts, Hispanic publications urged to improve market research and content sophistication, and advertisers assessing whether placement 'enhances the client's image' rather than assuming ethnic ownership alone suffices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designing content to attract women readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Content choices intended to reverse declines in women readership by covering topics and styles women report wanting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research indicates women want topics such as children's education (how children learn), time/money saving, safety/health, women in the workplace, social concerns, and family/personal relationships; they want information that is useful, easy to find, and deep, and they dislike insensitive invasion of privacy. Newspapers have created beats and story angles to be more relevant to women's daily lives while avoiding 'superwomen' portrayals that alienate readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governmental controls and press-freedom risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments exert controls over media via laws, regulations, licenses, taxes, and financing, and journalists face substantial press-freedom violations worldwide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In state-dominated or heavily regulated systems, control comes through financing or legal mechanisms. Even in more open countries, journalists face kidnapping, arrest, assault, death threats, and other harassment; these risks and legal frameworks shape what media can or will cover.
